record.paper_title: Monetary Stabilization in Cryptocurrencies—Design Approaches and Open Questions
record.original_question: Are all cryptocurrency soft pegs vulnerable to speculative attacks, or can a soft peg that relies solely on full proxy-collateralization or full self-collateralization be immune by guaranteeing enough collateral to buy back the entire money stock at any time?

evidence.quote:
The usefulness of soft pegs is disputed in economic liter-
ature. This standpoint is called the bipolar view [45], [46],
and is broadly supported by mainstream economists [45],
[47]–[49]. The bipolar view suggests that there are only
two long-term viable options for currency regimes that care
for exchange rates: hard pegs or ﬂoating with interventions.
Reasons given are short life expectancy of soft pegs and
vulnerability to speculative attacks [45].
Speculative attacks on soft pegs are known from traditional
central banking [50], [51], but the threat is equally applicable
to cryptocurrencies. This is especially relevant considering that
50 % of stablecoin projects plan on using soft pegs.

We do question though, if all kinds of soft pegs are equally
vulnerable in the case of cryptocurrencies. Soft-pegs relying
solely on full proxy and self-collateralization promise to
provide sufﬁcient collateral to buy back the complete stock
of money at any moment of time. This, in turn, makes them
immune to the above described attack [52].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a cryptocurrency that maintains a soft peg to a reference asset (i.e., a fixed target exchange rate that the issuer defends, but which may be abandoned or adjusted, as opposed to a hard peg enforced by an irrevocable mechanism). A speculative attack on such a peg is a coordinated action by market participants who short or redeem the pegged currency in sufficient volume to exhaust the issuer's defensive reserves and force a devaluation.

Distinguish the following collateralization regimes for a stablecoin of total outstanding money stock M (denominated in units of the peg target):

(a) Full proxy-collateralization: the issuer holds, in custody, reserves of the peg target (or assets denominated in it) of value at least M at all times, and these reserves are unconditionally available to redeem the currency at the pegged rate.

(b) Full self-collateralization: every unit of the stablecoin is backed by collateral, denominated in another crypto-asset, whose market value is maintained at or above M through on-chain over-collateralization and liquidation rules, and which can be liquidated to buy back the entire money stock at the pegged rate at any moment.

(c) Partial or fractional collateralization: reserves strictly less than M.

Question: Is every cryptocurrency soft peg necessarily vulnerable to a speculative attack, or do soft pegs operating under regime (a) or regime (b) constitute exceptions that are provably immune to speculative attack by virtue of being able to buy back the entire money stock at the pegged rate at any time? Formulate precise conditions on the collateral, redemption mechanism, and market microstructure under which such immunity holds, or exhibit a speculative-attack strategy that succeeds against any soft peg even under full proxy- or self-collateralization.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of whether fully collateralized soft pegs in cryptocurrencies are immune to speculative attacks remains an open design and economics question. Subsequent literature on stablecoins (e.g., analyses of DAI, MakerDAO, and algorithmic stablecoins, and post-2022 events such as the collapse of UST and stress on DAI) has shown that self-collateralized systems can still face runs and de-pegging episodes, but no consensus theoretical result establishes either universal vulnerability or universal immunity. The question is generally treated as still open.

status_evidence.title: Monetary Stabilization in Cryptocurrencies—Design Approaches and Open Questions
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses speculative attack vulnerability of soft pegs and questions whether fully proxy- or self-collateralized soft pegs are immune.
status_evidence.claim: The original framing presents this as an open design question.
